Commentary.Commentary: We are back with the chase. Australia Under-19 openers Will Malajczuk and Nitesh Samuel have walked out in the middle. Sebastian Morgan will be bowling the first over of this run chase for England Under-19.
... The Run Chase ...

Looking ahead - 235 and 253 have not been chased in the last couple of games here in Bulawayo. However, one game earlier, Sri Lanka successfully hunted down 262 against South Africa. Batting has tended to become more difficult as the day progresses at this venue, with inconsistent bounce and increasing assistance for the spinners making life tough for the batters. It is all set up for an intriguing chase with a place in the final on the line. Back in a bit for the chase.

A quick chat - England's Caleb Falconer thinks the total is pretty good, with enough in the pitch for England's bowlers. He believes that if they stay disciplined and execute well, they can get the job done. Falconer explains his role in the partnership with Thomas Rew, saying that his role was to keep Rew on strike and support him while he plays the big shots. He thinks the key for the bowlers is to keep it simple, hit the top of the stumps, bowl in the right areas, and keep all modes of dismissal in play.

Middle phase rebuild - The rebuild came through a 135-run stand between Caleb Falconer and skipper Thomas Rew. Unlike the game against New Zealand, where the English innings meandered through the middle phase, this time there was a healthier tempo. The boundaries flowed freely off the bat of Rew, who went on to reach his century in 97 balls. Rew’s departure proved to be the catalyst for Australia to pull things back as the English lower order found the spinners tough to get away.

A cagey start - Charles Lachmund and William Byrom were able to get the ball to swing early on, but the movement was inconsistent. Ben Dawkins fell early, while his namesake Ben Mayes and Joe Moores negotiated the opening burst from the Australian quicks. However, neither was able to convert their start into a substantial contribution, and England soon found themselves reduced to 60/3.

England Under-19 finish with 277! Australia will be pleased with how the final phase unfolded for them. At one stage, England looked set to push towards 300, but just 40 runs came from the last 7 overs, keeping them under 280. 277 is still a formidable total, though.
Leg bye! On a good length, tailing on the pads. Ahmed fails to flick and it rolls off the pads to point for a leg bye. England Under-19 end with 277 on the board in the Semi-Finals.

Commentary.Commentary: We are done with everything and the focus now shifts to cricket. The English openers, Ben Dawkins and Joe Moores, are out in the middle to open the innings. Charles Lachmund is all set with the ball in his hands to set the stage on fire for Australia Under-19. Dawkins to face the first ball. Two slips in place. Here we go!

We're all set for the pre-match formalities. The teams stride out behind the match officials and get lined up on either side of the officials for their respective national anthems. It will be England's first, followed by Australia's.

Charles Lachmund is buzzing with excitement - The Aussie pacer shares that they watched the India vs Pakistan game to learn about the local conditions, which differ from those in Namibia or Harare. Lachmund is thrilled with his wicket-taking performance and credits the team's bowling attack and calm captaincy for putting them in a good position. Mentions that he is looking forward to the captain's insights before the game.

A quick word - England's Ben Mayes says it feels brilliant to be in such form and credits the backing of his teammates for helping him score runs. He describes the tournament as a phenomenal event and is delighted to be able to continue his good form. According to Mayes, there is a strong belief within the group that any individual can win a game single-handedly, and even when someone is doubting themselves, the team rallies around them. Reflecting on his favourite moments of the tournament, Mayes points to England’s opening win against Pakistan as a standout. Although he did not make a major contribution with the bat, he says it felt very special given the magnitude of the contest heading into the competition. Speaking about the Under-19 pathway, he says it is inspiring to see how many players progress from the Lions setup into the senior England team, describing it as a clear stepping stone. He points to Jacob Bethell’s journey from the 2022 Under-19 World Cup to becoming a key player for England as a prime example.

PITCH REPORT - Lydia Greenway notes that pitch 4 will be used today. Adds that this is the same surface that was used for the England-Bangladesh game. Andy Flower joins her, and he says that the sun has been beating down on this strip, leaving the wicket very dry. Observes some straw-coloured grass in the centre, but given the dry patches around it, he feels that the surface will be inconsistent in terms of the bounce. He expects the batting conditions to be tricky and does not expect it to be a high-scoring game.

The captain of Australia Under-19 - Oliver Peake says they would have batted first as he feels there is a bit of inconsistent bounce and might stay low compared to Namibia, and admits they have to adapt to the conditions quickly. Reckons they are ready for this match. Expresses that they want to do what they have done so far in this tournament, enjoy every opportunity. Informs that William Byrom comes in as the only change.

The captain of England Under-19 - Thomas Rew has decided to bat first, citing previous game experience at the venue as a factor in their decision. He noted inconsistent bounce throughout the day and expected the pitch to spin, making it beneficial to set the tone early. Rew also mentioned that the team is feeling good after a rest day and training sessions, and there's just one change in the team with Alex Green being replaced by Alex French.

England Under-19 (Playing XI) - Ben Dawkins, Joe Moores, Ben Mayes, Thomas Rew (C/WK), Caleb Falconer, Ralphie Albert, Farhan Ahmed, Sebastian Morgan, James Minto, Manny Lumsden and Alex French (In for Alex Green).

Australia Under-19 (Playing XI) - Will Malajczuk, Nitesh Samuel, Steven Hogan, Oliver Peake (C), Alex Lee Young (WK), Jayden Draper, Aryan Sharma, Hayden Schiller, Naden Cooray, William Byrom (In for Ben Gordon) and Charles Lachmund.
TOSS - The flip of the coin comes down in favour of Thomas Rew. England Under-19 elect to BAT first.

The tactical battle - As these old foes collide, the game is expected to be won or lost in the early exchanges. Australia’s pace duo will look to attack the stumps early, while England’s aggressive openers, like Ben Dawkins, aim to exploit the powerplay restrictions. The dry Bulawayo pitch may also bring spinners like England’s Farhan Ahmed and Australia’s Charles Lachmund into a critical middle-over battle. With Australia eyeing their seventh Men's U19 World Cup final and England chasing their third, the stakes could not be higher for these young stars to prove their mettle in one of world cricket's most storied rivalries. England’s explosive batting and momentum - England arrives in the semi-finals with perhaps the most explosive batting lineup in the competition. Their campaign has been defined by massive scores, including an individual knock of 191 by Ben Mayes against Scotland. Captain Thomas Rew has led from the front, notably in an unbeaten 167-run partnership with Mayes to dismantle Zimbabwe. England’s bowlers have also stepped up, with Manny Lumsden claiming a five-wicket haul to secure their semi-final berth against New Zealand. While their batting is in red-hot form, they will need to ensure their discipline remains airtight against the defending champions.

Australia’s clinical path - The defending champions, led by Oliver Peake, have marched through the tournament with clinical efficiency. Australia topped Group A before navigating a challenging Super Six stage, which included a dominant victory over South Africa and a gritty 22-run win against the West Indies. Their success has been built on a balanced bowling attack featuring Charles Lachmund and William Byrom, who have consistently skittled oppositions for low totals. However, while their top order has been anchored reliably by Nitesh Samuel and Steven Hogan, the middle order faced its first real test against the West Indies, suggesting there is still room to sharpen their batting depth under sustained pressure.

Welcome, cricket fans - A high-octane encounter awaits us at the Queens Sports Club in Bulawayo. The stage is perfectly set for the first semi-final of the ICC Under-19 World Cup 2026 as arch-rivals Australia and England face off with a spot in the final on the line. Both teams enter this knockout clash with unblemished records, having won all five of their matches so far, ensuring that one side’s perfect streak will come to a heartbreaking end today.

The mini-Ashes battle in Bulawayo - What began with sixteen teams dreaming big has now narrowed to four who have earned the right to dream louder. The ICC Under-19 Cricket World Cup 2026 has moved through the group stage, survived the Super Six squeeze, and now stands at the semifinal doorstep. Australia and Afghanistan stormed through Group 1 with authority, while India and England emerged from Group 2 with equal conviction. The spotlight now shifts to Bulawayo, where Queens Sports Club sets the stage for a mouthwatering first semifinal. Billed as a mini Ashes, it fits the script perfectly. Rampaging Australia versus a high-flying England, both unbeaten, both brimming with confidence, and both convinced their name belongs in the final. Australia’s road here has been relentless. They swept aside Ireland, Japan and Sri Lanka in the group stage, before blowing South Africa away in the Super Sixes and then holding their nerve in a tight contest against West Indies. England have been no less dominant. Pakistan and Zimbabwe were brushed aside early, Scotland were flattened by a staggering 252 runs, and the Super Six brought clinical, no-nonsense wins over Bangladesh and New Zealand. The Kangaroos with spring in their steps - Seeing Australia this deep into a tournament is hardly a shock, whether it is the seniors, the juniors, or the women. The script has been familiar here too, do the damage with the ball first. In five games so far, they have bowled first four times. What really stands out is how nasty their bowling unit has been. Up front, Charles Lachmund and Will Bryom have stitched together a fearsome new ball partnership, one that has left batting orders scrambling for oxygen. Between them, they have picked up 21 wickets and bulldozed opposition one after another. Only once (against West Indies) have Australia failed to pick a single wicket in the Powerplay. As a result of such a clinical demolition job, the load from the batters has significantly eased up. Chases have been calm and controlled, with Australia never losing more than four wickets while hunting down a target. When they did bat first, the intent was just as sharp. Against West Indies, they tore into the attack to post 314, powered by a superb century from Oliver Peake. Nitesh Samuel and Steve Hogan have been the backbone of the batting, the only two Australians to cross 200 runs in the tournament. Will Malajczuk, meanwhile, has quietly gone about his job, delivering consistency when it has mattered. However, with the top order doing most of the scoring, the middle order has barely been tested and remains a big unknown going into the knockout clash. The Three Lions have roared - England, meanwhile, have won in variety. They have won big, won close, while setting a total, and have defended them as well. There were brief tests while batting first against Pakistan and New Zealand, but the record-breaking 404 against Scotland sent their net run rate through the roof. At the heart of it all is Ben Mayes. With two fifties and a century, he sits atop the run charts, averaging a ridiculous 93.75, and owning the highest individual score of the tournament with a brutal 191 against Scotland. The middle order, though, has found real steel in captain Thomas Rew and Caleb Falconer, who have repeatedly steadied and shaped innings. The only real soft spot has been right at the top. England’s opening partnerships have blown hot and cold, averaging just 23.6, leaving a small but noticeable chink in an otherwise solid armour. With the ball too, England have been just as ruthless, bowling out four of their five opponents so far. Manny Lumsden has led the charge, highlighted by a sensational 5/17 against New Zealand. Around him, Ralphie Albert and Farhan Ahmed have repeatedly applied the squeeze through the middle overs, keeping batters under constant pressure. In fact, apart from Zimbabwe, they have not allowed any other side even to reach the 200-run mark, a stat that underlines their remarkable consistency. The big question now is whether that control and cutting-edge can hold up against their fiercest rivals when it matters most. Big stakes, old grudges - Australia walk into this semifinal chasing a fifth title at this level. England, on the other hand, are playing catch-up with history. Their last triumph came way back in 1998, when they last won the trophy. The head-to-head numbers lean Australia’s way heavily. They have won four of the last five clashes against their old rivals, and in World Cups, England have not beaten Australia since 2014. History favours the Aussies, but knockout cricket has a habit of asking uncomfortable questions. Let’s see who makes it to the finale. Should be a cracker of a game.
